name: Dog
summary: Loyal, social companions that need daily exercise, training and lots of attention.
size: Small to giant depending on breed
diet: Feed a complete dog food suited to age (puppy, adult, senior). Puppies eat 3-4 small meals a day, adults 2 meals.
Fresh clean water must always be available.
Cooked plain chicken, rice, boiled egg and carrots are safe occasional extras.
Treats should be under 10% of daily calories.
housing: A quiet bed or crate in a warm, dry corner away from drafts.
Secure yard or leash walks; dogs must not be left tied all day.
Provide shade and cool water in summer; a warm blanket in winter.
daily: 30-90 minutes of walking or play depending on breed.
Two feeding times and fresh water changes.
Short training sessions (5-10 minutes) and affection.
grooming: Brush 1-3 times a week (daily for long coats).
Bath every 4-6 weeks with dog shampoo only.
Trim nails monthly and brush teeth 2-3 times a week.
Check ears weekly for dirt or bad smell.
health: Vaccinate: puppy series, then yearly boosters (including rabies).
Deworm regularly and use tick/flea prevention.
Vet check-up once a year; twice a year for seniors.
Warning signs: vomiting more than once, not eating for a day, limping, bloated belly, heavy panting.
training: Start at 8 weeks: sit, come, stay, leave it.
Use rewards and praise; never hit or shout.
Socialize puppies early with people, sounds and other dogs.
Teach toilet routine: out after waking, eating and playing.
tips: Never leave a dog in a closed car.
Microchip or ID tag helps if the dog gets lost.
Choose a breed that fits your home size and energy.

name: Cat
summary: Independent but affectionate pets that are clean, playful and good for apartments.
diet: Cats are obligate carnivores: feed high-protein cat food (wet food plus dry).
Kittens eat 3-4 times a day; adults 2 times.
Always keep fresh water; many cats prefer a fountain or wide bowl.
Cooked chicken or fish in small amounts is fine; cow milk can upset their stomach.
housing: A clean litter box in a quiet spot, scooped daily and fully washed weekly.
A scratching post, a high perch and a cozy bed.
Keep windows and balconies safe with nets.
daily: 15-30 minutes of play with a wand toy or ball.
Scoop the litter, refresh water, feed meals.
Quiet time and gentle petting.
grooming: Brush weekly (daily for long-haired cats).
Trim nails every 2-3 weeks.
Cats rarely need baths; wipe with a damp cloth if dirty.
Dental care: brush or use dental treats.
health: Kitten vaccines, then yearly boosters; rabies vaccine too.
Deworm and use flea control.
Spay or neuter around 5-6 months unless breeding.
Warning signs: hiding for long, straining in the litter box, not eating, constant vomiting.
training: Place the kitten in the litter box after meals; they learn fast.
Redirect scratching to a post with treats.
Use clicker or treats for simple tricks and carrier comfort.
tips: Indoor cats live longer.
Introduce new pets slowly.
Give each cat its own litter box (plus one extra).

name: Rabbit
summary: Gentle, social herbivores that need lots of hay, space to hop and a calm home.
diet: 80% unlimited fresh hay (timothy or grass hay) - essential for teeth and digestion.
A handful of leafy greens daily (coriander, romaine, mint).
Small portion of rabbit pellets; carrots and fruit only as rare treats.
Fresh water in a heavy bowl or bottle.
housing: Large pen or hutch at least 4x the rabbit's length, plus daily time outside it.
Keep cool: rabbits overheat above 28 C. Avoid direct sun.
Soft flooring (not wire) and a hiding box.
daily: 3-4 hours of free roaming in a safe area.
Fresh hay and greens twice a day.
Spot clean the toilet corner, full clean weekly.
grooming: Brush weekly, daily when molting.
Trim nails every 4-6 weeks.
Never bathe in water; spot clean only.
health: Teeth grow constantly; hay and chew sticks keep them worn.
Annual vet check and vaccines where available.
Warning signs: no droppings for 12 hours, not eating, head tilt, wet chin. These are emergencies.
training: Rabbits can learn litter training and their name.
Be patient; let them come to you rather than picking them up suddenly.
Support the back legs when lifting.
tips: Rabbits are happier in bonded pairs.
Bunny-proof wires.
They hide pain well, so watch their behavior.

name: Parrot
summary: Intelligent, social birds that need a big cage, mental stimulation and daily interaction.
diet: Quality seed and pellet mix as the base.
Fresh vegetables and fruit daily (carrot, spinach, apple without seeds).
Cuttlebone or mineral block for calcium.
Fresh water changed every day.
housing: Cage wide enough for the bird to fully spread wings and climb.
Place at eye level in a bright room away from kitchen fumes.
Perches of different thickness, toys and a bath dish.
Cover at night for 10-12 hours of sleep.
daily: 1-2 hours out of the cage in a safe room.
Talk, whistle and play with them.
Remove old food; wash bowls.
grooming: Offer a shallow bath or light misting weekly.
Nails and beak usually stay healthy with perches; a vet can trim if needed.
Feathers and wings should only be clipped by a professional.
health: Fluffed feathers, sitting at the bottom, discharge from eyes or tail bobbing are warning signs.
Annual avian vet check.
Keep away from Teflon fumes, smoke and strong sprays; these can kill birds.
training: Build trust first: sit near the cage and talk softly.
Step-up training with a treat.
Repeat words clearly; reward with attention.
tips: Birds need company; lonely parrots get stressed.
Rotate toys to avoid boredom.
Never leave in direct hot sun.

name: Hamster
summary: Tiny, nocturnal pets that are easy to keep but need a big cage and a wheel.
diet: Hamster seed mix or pellets (1-2 tablespoons daily).
Small pieces of fresh veggies: carrot, cucumber, broccoli.
Occasional boiled egg or mealworm for protein.
Fresh water in a drip bottle.
housing: Large cage with deep bedding for burrowing (paper bedding, not cedar).
A solid-surface exercise wheel (at least 20 cm for dwarf, 28 cm for Syrian).
House solitary Syrian hamsters alone.
daily: Evening play and feeding as they wake.
Remove spoiled food from their hidden stash.
Spot clean weekly.
grooming: Offer a sand bath; never water.
Nails wear down naturally on wheel and toys.
health: Wet tail (diarrhea), overgrown teeth, weight loss and lethargy need a vet.
Keep temperature stable, 18-24 C.
training: Let them sniff your hand first and handle gently over a soft surface.
Use treats to build trust.
tips: Never wake a sleeping hamster suddenly.
Hamsters can bite when frightened.

name: Guinea Pig
summary: Gentle, chatty small pets that need vitamin C, hay and a friend.
diet: Unlimited hay daily.
Vitamin C-rich vegetables: bell pepper, parsley, kale.
Small amount of guinea pig pellets with added vitamin C.
Fresh water always.
housing: Large cage or pen, at least 0.7 square metres for two animals.
Soft bedding and a hide house.
Keep away from heat and drafts.
daily: Fresh veggies and hay twice a day.
An hour of floor time.
Spot clean daily; full clean weekly.
grooming: Brush long-haired breeds daily.
Trim nails monthly.
Bathe only when needed with guinea pig safe shampoo.
health: They cannot make vitamin C; deficiency causes scurvy.
Watch for sneezing, weight loss, overgrown teeth.
Annual vet check by an exotic-animal vet.
training: Hand-feed veggies to build trust.
Talk gently; they respond to routine.
tips: Keep them in pairs.
Hay is not optional.

name: Fish
summary: Calm, beautiful pets; success depends on clean, stable water.
diet: Feed good flake or pellet food made for your species.
Feed only what they finish in 2 minutes, once or twice a day.
Overfeeding is the number one cause of dirty tanks.
housing: Bigger tanks are more stable: goldfish need 75 L+ each, betta 20 L+.
Use a filter, heater for tropical fish and dechlorinated water.
Cycle the tank (grow beneficial bacteria) for 4-6 weeks before adding fish.
daily: Feed and check fish look active.
Check temperature and that the filter works.
grooming: Change 20-30% of the water weekly.
Rinse filter media in old tank water, not tap water.
Wipe algae from glass.
health: White spots, torn fins, gasping at the surface or clamped fins mean poor water or disease.
Test ammonia, nitrite and nitrate regularly.
Quarantine new fish for 2 weeks.
training: Fish learn feeding time and may eat from your hand.
tips: Bettas live alone.
Never dump all water at once.

name: Turtle
summary: Long-lived reptiles needing UV light, a basking spot and clean water or a proper habitat.
diet: Water turtles: turtle pellets plus leafy greens and occasional insects or fish.
Tortoises: mostly leafy greens, weeds and some vegetables; little fruit.
Provide calcium (cuttlebone) and keep a UVB light.
housing: Aquatic turtles need a large tank (10 gallons per inch of shell) with filter and dry basking dock.
Tortoises need a spacious pen with hide and substrate for burrowing.
UVB lamp 10-12 hours daily; replace every 6-12 months.
daily: Feed and refresh water.
Ensure basking heat 30-35 C and UVB working.
grooming: Do not scrub the shell hard; a soft brush is enough.
Change tank water often.
health: Soft shell, swollen eyes, runny nose or refusing food need a reptile vet.
Wash hands after handling; turtles can carry Salmonella.
training: Turtles learn feeding routine; handle rarely.
tips: Turtles can outlive you - plan long term.
Check local laws before buying.

name: Chicken
summary: Productive backyard birds that give eggs and need a safe coop and daily feed.
diet: Layer feed with calcium for hens, chick starter for chicks.
Kitchen scraps (veggies, grains) in moderation; clean water always.
Provide grit and oyster shell.
housing: Predator-proof coop with 0.4 sq m per bird indoors and run space outside.
Perches, nest boxes (1 per 4 hens) and good ventilation.
Dry bedding such as straw or wood shavings.
daily: Let out in the morning, collect eggs, check water and feed.
Lock the coop at dusk.
grooming: Provide a dust bath area.
Check for mites and lice monthly.
health: Vaccinate against common poultry diseases (Newcastle, Marek's).
Deworm regularly.
Isolate any sick bird immediately.
training: Hens learn to come when called with treats.
tips: Keep feed in sealed containers to avoid rodents.
Clean the coop weekly.

name: Goat
summary: Hardy, curious farm animals that give milk and need dry shelter and good forage.
diet: Good hay, browse (leaves, shrubs) and clean water.
Mineral supplement made for goats; grain in small amounts for milking or growing goats.
Introduce new feed slowly.
housing: Dry, draft-free shelter and a strong fence.
Raised platforms to climb and rest.
Keep dry bedding; goats dislike mud and rain.
daily: Grazing or browsing 6-8 hours, fresh water, health check by eye.
Milking twice a day for dairy goats.
grooming: Trim hooves every 6-8 weeks.
Brush coat occasionally.
health: Vaccinate (CD&T) and deworm per vet advice.
Watch for diarrhea, bloat, lameness and loss of appetite.
Ask a livestock vet about local diseases.
training: Goats learn routines, leading and milking stand easily.
tips: Goats are herd animals; keep at least two.
Fence must be tall and strong.

name: Ferret
summary: Playful, curious carnivores that need high-protein food and plenty of out-of-cage time.
diet: High-quality ferret food or a meat-based diet with high protein and fat.
No fruit, sugar or vegetables in large amounts.
housing: Multi-level cage with hammocks and a litter corner.
At least 4 hours out of the cage daily in a ferret-proofed room.
daily: Play, feeding twice or more, litter cleaning.
grooming: Bathe rarely (every 1-3 months).
Trim nails every 2 weeks and clean ears.
health: Annual vaccines and vet check; ferrets are prone to adrenal disease.
Keep cool; they overheat easily.
training: Litter training works with patience; use treats for tricks.
avoid: Small rubber items they might swallow
tips: Check local laws.
Ferrets sleep up to 18 hours a day.
